target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students interested in STEM

sections.title: Welcome to the Rubber-Sheet World
lecture_lines: Welcome to Topology, the study of rubber-sheet geometry.
Imagine a shape like this simple square outline.
It can smoothly morph into a circle without tearing.
animations: Fade in the text 'TOPOLOGY' in a light blue color (#56B4E9) at the center of the screen.
Transform the text 'TOPOLOGY' into a simple square outline with a blue stroke (#0072B2).
Morph the square outline into a perfect circle outline while maintaining the same blue stroke color (#0072B2).

sections.title: Prerequisite: Continuous Deformation
lecture_lines: We follow strict rules called "continuous deformations."
You can stretch, bend, or shrink any shape freely.
However, tearing holes or gluing parts is strictly forbidden.
animations: Display a horizontal yellow line segment (#F0E442) in the center.
Smoothly bend and stretch the yellow line into a complex, winding curve (#F0E442).
Display a red 'X' mark (#D55E00) over a dashed line representing a 'cut' to indicate tearing is forbidden.

sections.title: Homeomorphism: The Coffee Mug Paradox
lecture_lines: Mathematicians use the word "homeomorphism" for topological equality.
If shape A can morph into B, they are homeomorphs.
Take this classic example: a coffee mug and a doughnut.
The handle's hole is the only thing that really matters.
To a topologist, they are the same geometric object.
animations: Draw a white 2D outline representing a coffee mug (#FFFFFF) with a distinct handle.
Change the handle's stroke color to orange (#E69F00) to highlight its importance.
Morph the mug outline into a torus (doughnut) shape (#FFFFFF), with the handle becoming the central hole.
Pulse the central hole of the torus with an orange glow (#E69F00) to show its origin.
Display the label 'HOMEOMORPHISM' in bold orange text (#E69F00) above the shape.

sections.title: Topological Invariants: The 'Genus'
lecture_lines: We classify shapes using properties that never change, called invariants.
The "genus" counts the number of holes in a surface.
A sphere has genus zero, having no holes at all.
A torus has genus one, like a wedding ring.
You can't turn a sphere into a torus without tearing.
animations: Show a blue sphere (#56B4E9) on the left labeled 'Genus 0' and a green torus (#009E73) in the center labeled 'Genus 1'.
Show a purple double-torus (#CC79A7) on the right labeled 'Genus 2'.
Highlight the holes in each shape (0, 1, and 2 respectively) using a white flash (#FFFFFF).
Morph a 3D-looking cube into the blue sphere to show they are both Genus 0.
Display the summary text 'Genus is an Invariant' in white (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: Real-World Application: Network Topology
lecture_lines: Subway systems often start as messy geographic maps.
Topology transforms them into clean, readable schematics.
We focus only on paths connecting specific stations.
Distorting the map doesn't break these vital connections.
In this network, connectivity is the only invariant.
animations: Display a realistic city map with many nodes and messy, curved streets in gray (#999999).
Transform the map into a clean schematic where streets are only horizontal, vertical, or 45-degree angles.
Highlight a specific path between two nodes in bright blue (#0072B2).
Stretch and distort the schematic map while keeping all nodes and path connections unchanged.
Display the text 'CONNECTIVITY IS INVARIANT' in white (#FFFFFF) at the bottom.

sections.title: Summary: The Big Picture
lecture_lines: Topology shifts our focus from measurements to structural connections.
We identify deep patterns in DNA, data, and galaxies.
In this flexible world, continuity is the ultimate rule.
animations: Show two labeled 'buckets': 'Genus 0' (blue, #56B4E9) and 'Genus 1' (green, #009E73).
Animate a sphere and a cube moving into the 'Genus 0' bucket (#56B4E9).
Animate a mug and a torus moving into the 'Genus 1' bucket (#009E73).
